query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin, conformal alumina coating via atomic layer deposition (ALD) on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form a robust protective barrier that significantly reduces oxygen ingress during high‐temperature exposure without degrading its intrinsic mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultrathin alumina coating by ALD to the alloy’s surface.
generation.conditions: Expose coated samples to an oxidizing environment (e.g., air) at around 1000 °C for 100–200 hours while conducting tensile tests at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: The ALD-deposited alumina layer acts as a passivation barrier that physically limits oxygen diffusion into the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The alumina coating minimizes oxygen ingress and subsequent internal oxidation by providing an oxygen-impermeable layer, thereby preserving the alloy’s microstructure and its beneficial mechanical properties at high temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to show significantly reduced oxide scale growth and lower oxygen penetration without a measurable loss in the alloy’s room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength compared to the untreated cast state.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, which under high-temperature oxidizing exposure suffers from rapid oxide formation that compromises its integrity, despite its useful mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This improvement is predicted specifically under high-temperature (≈1000 °C) oxidizing conditions with exposure times on the order of 100–200 hours and at tensile strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹. The coating’s effectiveness outside these boundaries remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness, adhesion quality, and long-term durability of the ALD alumina coating under cyclic thermal/mechanical loading require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of cast HfNbTaTiZr samples: one with the ultrathin ALD alumina coating and one uncoated control. Subject both groups to continuous exposure at 1000 °C under air for 150 hours while simultaneously applying tensile loading at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
measurements: Quantify oxide scale thickness and composition via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
Determine oxygen diffusion profiles near the surface using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
Assess mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility) through standardized high-temperature tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the ALD-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxygen ingress and oxide scale formation, or if their high-temperature mechanical performance (ductility and yield strength) is degraded relative to that of the untreated samples under identical testing conditions.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. chosen.lever: protective surface coating to inhibit oxygen ingress
chosen.technique: atomic layer deposition (ALD) to apply a nano-scale, oxygen-impermeable oxide coating (such as alumina)
chosen.conditions: Testing the intervention at 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere with prolonged exposure (e.g., 100–200 hours) while subjecting samples to tensile loading at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹
chosen.why: This move directly inverts the niche of poor oxygen resistance by introducing a protective surface barrier through a well-established surface engineering technique. The ALD-deposited coating is designed to prevent oxygen diffusion into the high-entropy alloy without modifying its intrinsically favorable mechanical properties, thus addressing the performance limitation in a targeted and minimal manner.
